Sign up for free Δ But lawmakers swiftly depleted the fund during the early months of the Great Recession and were forced to make steep spending cuts, borrow money at expensive rates and use accounting gimmicks to weather the rest of the crisis. Under then-Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, a Republican, the state Legislature slashed health and welfare funding, scrapped tax credits, furloughed state employees (https://web.archive.org/web/20090809224605/http://www.dpa.ca.gov/news/news/2008/20081106-01.htm) and delayed payments (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2018/3910/recession-recovery-121318.pdf) to schools and local governments. In 2014, as the state’s economy rebounded, then-Gov. Jerry Brown, a Democrat, urged that the state save more. He and the Legislature championed Prop. 2, a bipartisan ballot measure that required the state to save more aggressively and limited when lawmakers could withdraw from the reserves. Nearly 70% of voters approved it. “When the pendulum swings again, we won’t be forced to raise taxes or make the kinds of harsh cuts that were all too common in recent years,” Brown said in a 2014 op-ed (https://www.sfgate.com/politics/article/Jerry-Brown-preaches-for-Prop-2-by-talking-up-5812922.php) stumping for the reform. The law requires the state to set aside 1.5% of its general fund revenue and any spikes in capital gains tax revenue each year, with half deposited into the reserves and the other half to pay down state debts. It also made it harder for the state to spend the reserves and carved out portions of the savings for schools. Under the law (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&division&title&part&chapter&article=XVI), state lawmakers can withdraw from the reserves only when the governor declares a budget emergency and decides that the state is not expected to collect enough revenue in the upcoming fiscal year to match the spending in the three previous budget years. A majority of state lawmakers must vote to ratify the budget emergency. If approved, they are allowed to withdraw up to half of the rainy day fund balance at once, unless they already withdrew half the balance in the previous budget year and still need to take out more. There are no limits on what lawmakers can use the funds for. Bigger reserve = more to spend? Prop. 2 would maintain those withdrawal rules, which critics say would give future governors broad authority to spend down the reserves instead of reining in spending. “The rainy day fund can be invaded even when it’s not raining, simply because spending isn’t as high as it was within the prior three years,” wrote David Crane (https://sfstandard.com/opinion/2026/09/14/newsom-rainy-day-fund-prop-2/), a former economic adviser to Schwarzenegger and founder of Govern for California, a nonprofit fundraising powerhouse (https://calmatters.org/politics/2022/08/california-campaign-finance-donor-network/) that aims to “counter special interest influence.” “Unless the withdrawal rules change, a larger reserve just lets governors bake in spending based on optimistic forecasts, knowing they can always dip into reserves if revenue falls short.” In an interview with CalMatters, Gabriel stressed that voters approved those rules in 2014 and emphasized that the measure has bipartisan support. He also dismissed the criticism that the state should just spend less during downturns, likening it to telling families to eat less or downsize instead of dipping into their savings when they fall on hard times. “I think (the concern) is very misplaced,” he said. “(Prop. 2) is recommended by the experts, because it matches the common-sense wisdom of California families.” READ NEXT What to know about California’s other tax-the-rich measure: Prop. 3 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-3-california/) October 21, 2026 This institute could get $4 billion from a ballot measure. Proposition 2
Raise limit on rainy day fund deposits
This constitutional amendment would allow the state to deposit up to 20% of its general fund tax revenue in the state’s reserves, up from the current ceiling of 10%. The deposits would not count toward the voter-approved Gann Limit, which caps the amount state lawmakers can spend each year and requires excess funds to be returned to the people. It also authorizes spending some tax revenue to pay down California’s $20 billion federal unemployment insurance debt. The California Legislature placed this measure on the ballot.

One area Democrats, GOP agree: California needs a larger rainy day fund

By Jesse Gabriel and Josh Hoover, Special for CalMatters

This commentary was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

Guest Commentary written by

At a moment when Californians can't agree on much, we've found common ground on something that matters: how the state saves for hard times.

One of us is a Democrat. The other is a Republican. We are united about Proposition 2, because this measure isn't about partisan politics. It's about basic fiscal responsibility, and it was developed by the people who understand California's budget best.

California has one of the largest and most dynamic economies in the world. It's also one of the most volatile. The state ranks fifth in the nation in revenue volatility because of our tax structure, but only 29th in the size of its budget reserves.

When the good times roll, state revenue pours in. When the economy faces challenges, the state is often forced into abrupt, painful cuts to programs Californians rely on: healthcare, higher education, public safety and safety net services.

Seniors, students and working families bear the brunt, often with little warning.

Prop. 2 fixes that imbalance. It doubles the size of the state's rainy day fund and requires California to save more during strong budget years, so we're not caught flat-footed when the next downturn hits.

This is a structural budget fix without raising taxes to save more. It’s the type of budgetary planning we need to protect our future.

This isn't a new or radical idea. It builds directly on a framework voters approved in 2014. And it reflects more than a decade of experience with how that fund has actually worked.

Prop. 2 didn’t start with politicians. It was born from budget experts, not special interests. 

The Legislative Analyst's Office, California's nonpartisan fiscal watchdog, recommended its reforms, which developed during legislative hearings with input from the Department of Finance, independent fiscal experts and business leaders.

But its earliest supporters were firefighters, small business advocates, healthcare providers and education leaders — people who see firsthand what happens when reserves run dry and cuts land on hospitals, schools and emergency response. 

That list has since grown because state leaders and fiscal experts from across the political spectrum have lived through what happens when California doesn't save enough.

A stronger rainy day fund would make California more fiscally credible to taxpayers. States that save responsibly don't just weather downturns better; they also borrow more cheaply and give families and businesses more confidence that the state can keep its commitments, even when the economy turns. 

That's the real case for Prop 2. California is safer, steadier and more trustworthy when it saves like it means it.

Saving responsibly is not a partisan value. It's common sense. California's budget shouldn't lurch from boom to bust. Prop. 2 gives us a better way forward.

PROPOSED AMENDMENTS TO ARTICLE XVI
First—(a) This measure shall be known, and may be
cited, as the Save for California’s Future Act.
(b) The Legislature finds and declares all of the
following:
(1) California families understand that responsible
financial planning requires setting aside savings during
good times to prepare for unexpected challenges and
economic downturns. The State of California should
follow the same commonsense principle.
(2) Californians expect their government to manage
public finances responsibly, prudently, and with an eye
toward future generations. Maintaining adequate
reserves helps ensure that essential public services
remain available when they are needed most.
(3) California’s economy is among the largest and
most dynamic in the world, but it is also subject to
economic cycles, fluctuations in revenue, natural
disasters, public health emergencies, and other
unforeseen events that can place significant strain on
the state budget.
(4) When state revenues decline during economic
downturns, insufficient reserves can force difficult
choices that disrupt essential programs and services
relied upon by California families, students, seniors,
veterans, workers, and businesses.
(5) Building and maintaining strong budget reserves
during periods of economic growth helps protect
Californians from sudden reductions in essential
services and reduces the need for drastic corrective
actions during periods of fiscal stress.
(6) Sound financial planning requires looking beyond
the next fiscal year and preparing for future challenges
before they arise. Just like families save for
emergencies and unexpected expenses, California
should save during good years to protect schools,
public safety, and essential services during tough
times.
(7) Strong reserve policies promote fiscal stability,
improve public confidence in state government,
support long-term economic growth, and help preserve
California’s ability to respond effectively to
emergencies and economic downturns.
(8) Proposition 98 was enacted by the voters in 1988
to provide a minimum funding level for schools. Nothing
in this act is intended to change the calculation or
106 | Text of Proposed Laws
funding of the minimum guarantee under Section 8 of
Article XVI.
(c) It is therefore the intent of the Legislature to
strengthen the state’s commitment to responsible
budgeting, long-term financial planning, and prudent
savings by enhancing California’s budget reserves and
ensuring that the state is better prepared for future
economic challenges. Strengthening reserves is an
investment in California’s future and in future
generations.

Proposition 2
Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
Analysis of Measure
Background
The State Budget
How Does the State Spend Its Money? This year, the state plans to spend about $250 billion from the General Fund to pay for services to the public. The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services. About half of this spending is for schools, community colleges, and the state's public universities. (The State Constitution sets a minimum spending level for schools and community colleges.) About another one-third of state spending is for health and human services programs, mainly for the state's low-income health insurance program, Medi-Cal. The rest goes mostly to prisons, courts, and other state services.
How Does the State Raise Revenue? The income tax is the state's largest tax. It pays for most spending from the General Fund. Other major taxes include the corporation tax and the sales tax. Much of the income tax is paid by high-income taxpayers, whose incomes often include gains from stocks and other investments.
State Revenues Are Unpredictable. State revenues go up and down a lot from year to year. This is because revenues depend on how the economy and stock market are doing. When things are going well, revenues can grow quickly. When things are going badly, like during a recession or a stock market crash, revenues can decline by tens of billions of dollars. During a bad recession or market crash, total revenue declines over a few years can equal 50 percent or more of annual General Fund revenues.
The State Must Meet Certain Budgeting Requirements Each Year. The State Constitution requires the Legislature to pass a balanced budget each year. This means the state cannot adopt a budget that spends more money than is available. In addition, the State Constitution limits how much tax revenue the state can spend. This limit is called the "state appropriations limit." Certain kinds of spending-like infrastructure-do not count toward the limit. All other spending, including money put into reserves, does count toward the limit.
Reserves
Reserves Allow the State to Maintain Spending When Revenues Decline. The state puts money into reserves when the economy is doing well. This means that money is saved instead of being spent on public programs during these periods of time. When the economy gets worse and revenues decline, the state uses reserves to help maintain spending on public programs. Reserves help the state avoid some spending cuts, tax increases, and borrowing to balance the budget. Currently, the state has about $20 billion in reserves that can be used for any public program.
State Constitution Requires the State to Save Money in the "Rainy Day Fund." The State Constitution requires the state to deposit 0.75 percent of General Fund tax revenues in the state's main rainy day fund, which is called the Budget Stabilization Account, each year. Money in the rainy day fund can be used for any state program. In addition, the state must put more money into the rainy day fund in years when revenue from taxes on investment gains is higher than normal. During a budget emergency, the state can stop making deposits and/or take money out of the rainy day fund.
Savings Are No Longer Required Once the Rainy Day Fund Reaches a Certain Level. Once money in the rainy day fund reaches 10 percent of General Fund taxes, the state is no longer required to make additional deposits. The money that would have gone into the rainy day fund instead must be spent on infrastructure (like highways and housing).
Debt
The State Has Different Kinds of Debts. The state has more than $250 billion in debts. These include debt for infrastructure and pension and retiree health benefits earned by state employees. The state also sometimes borrows money from other state funds to help pay General Fund costs. State debts are repaid over time, usually according to a schedule or plan. Each year, the state makes payments toward its debts.
State Constitution Requires the State to Make Extra Debt Payments Toward Pension and Health Benefits. The State Constitution requires the state to make extra debt payments above those normally made each year. The amount of these extra debt payments is the same as the amount initially deposited into the rainy day fund each year. The state may only use these extra debt payments to pay down long-term pension and retiree health care debts. Making extra payments toward these debts saves the state money in the long run.
Extra Debt Payments Optional After 2030. The requirement for extra debt payments ends in 2030. After that, the Legislature and the Governor could decide to deposit the money for extra debt payments into the rainy day fund instead. Or, the Legislature and the Governor could make smaller extra debt payments and put the rest of the money into the rainy day fund.
Proposal
Save More in the Rainy Day Fund. Proposition 2 requires the state to make deposits into the rainy day fund until it reaches 20 percent of General Fund taxes (instead of 10 percent of General Fund taxes). In addition, the state would make even larger deposits in years when revenues from taxes on investment gains are very high, like when the stock market is booming.
Extend and Expand Extra Debt Payments. Proposition 2 also requires the state to make extra debt payments through 2040 (instead of through 2030). These debt payments would be the same as the amount initially deposited into the rainy day fund each year. In addition, the amount set aside for extra debt payments could be used for an expanded set of purposes. Specifically, these payments could be used to make required payments to schools and community colleges, repay borrowing from other state funds, and repay certain loans from the federal government.
Change How Rainy Day Fund Deposits Count Toward the State Appropriations Limit. Deposits into the rainy day fund would not count toward the state appropriations limit. Instead, the money would count toward the limit when it is taken out.
Change How Other Deposits Count Toward the State Appropriations Limit. The state has an account to set aside funds when revenues are surging. By setting these funds aside, the state can avoid overspending when revenue estimates are particularly uncertain. Under Proposition 2, deposits into this account also would not count toward the state appropriations limit. Instead, the money would count toward the limit when it is taken out. This exclusion could not be larger than 10 percent of General Fund taxes in each year.
Fiscal Effects
Budget Reserves Would Be Higher. By continuing to require deposits into the rainy day fund until the balance reaches 20 percent of General Fund taxes, the state would save more over time. In addition, by depositing more money when revenues are surging, the state likely would save more in the rainy day fund in certain years. More reserves would make balancing the budget somewhat easier when revenues decline.
Possibly More Debt Payments. By requiring the state to make extra debt payments through 2040, the state might make more debt payments than it would without Proposition 2.
Yes/No Statement
A YES vote on this measure means: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would change. As a result, state budget reserves would be higher. The state also would be required to make extra debt payments for longer.
A NO vote on this measure means: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would not change.
Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact
State budget reserves would be higher.

Proposition 2: Rainy Day Fund
Proposition 2: Rainy Day Fund
Proposition 2: Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund. Legislative Constitutional Amendment
Additional Titles
Budget Stabilization Account Cap Increase and Gann Limit Changes Amendment
Rainy day Fund
Raise limit on rainy day fund deposits
Summary
Proposition 2 was placed on the ballot by the California Legislature as Assembly Constitutional Amendment 20 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA20&utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email) The amendment was introduced on June 25, 2026 and it passed the state Assembly by a vote of 59-8, with 12 not voting. It passed the state Senate by a vote of 29-2, with nine not voting.
Proposition 2 on the November 2026 ballot would amend the State Constitution (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codesTOCSelected.xhtml?tocCode=CONS&tocTitle=+California+Constitution+-+CONS) by changing California’s rainy day fund rules to build larger reserves and better protect public services during economic downturns and other budget emergencies. Specifically, it would require the state to make deposits into the fund until it reaches 20 percent of General Fund taxes (instead of the current 10 percent of General Fund taxes).
It would also expand the types of state debt that can be repaid with General Fund money set aside each year and require the extra debt payments through 2040 (instead of the current date of 2030). In addition, Prop. 2 would change how certain reserves are treated under the state spending cap, or “Gann Limit (https://www.cde.ca.gov/fg/ac/gl/),” making it easier to save more money when revenues are strong. F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 2 would allow California to build a larger financial cushion by raising the maximum size of the state’s rainy day fund. It would also direct a greater share of unusually strong revenues into savings during high-revenue years. Having more money set aside could give the state greater flexibility during economic downturns or other periods when tax collections fall short of expectations.
Proposition 2 would extend requirements for additional state debt payments through 2040. As a result, California could pay down more of its outstanding debts and long-term financial obligations than it otherwise would under current rules.

YES: A “yes” vote supports changing California’s rainy day fund rules to allow larger reserves, increase deposits when revenues are strong, extend required debt payments through 2040, and change how certain reserves are treated under the state spending limit. It would also allow the governor’s May budget revision to serve as a declaration of a budget emergency when certain conditions are met.

Critics say it would only allow state leaders to spend more in the future. The question Proposition 2 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-2-rainy-day-fund/) poses to California voters is simple: Should the state be able to save more money when its economy is booming? The ballot measure, dubbed the Save for California’s Future Act (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260aca20), seeks to shore up California’s rainy day fund by allowing state lawmakers to sock away up to 20% of the state’s general fund tax revenue — double the current ceiling of 10%. It would also require the state to save a bigger share of the gains when revenue is growing faster. Proponents, including Gov. Gavin Newsom and Democratic lawmakers, say the state needs a bigger savings account to weather its volatile economy. Because California’s tax revenue depends so much on wealthy residents’ stock earnings, the state budget is often caught in a boom-or-bust cycle (https://calmatters.org/explainers/california-budget-whiplash/) at the mercy of the market. In recent years, the state has seen robust tax revenue from an AI-fueled economy, which has helped state leaders avoid or delay painful cuts (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/05/gavin-newsom-final-budget-plan/) to social services even when they projected significant deficits. But economists have consistently warned the boom may not last, and the federal budget cuts to healthcare and welfare programs this year deepened that uncertainty. This voter guide has everything you need to know Supporters pitched Prop. 2 as a common sense solution, noting the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office, which advises state lawmakers, has long recommended the state set aside funding for downturns. The measure is endorsed by a bipartisan coalition of groups (https://www.yesonprop2.com/#endorsements), including labor unions, hospital associations and chambers of commerce. “It doubles the size of the state’s rainy day fund and requires California to save more during strong budget years, so we’re not caught flat-footed when the next downturn hits,” wrote (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/10/rainy-day-fund-california-proposition/) Assembly Budget Chair Jesse Gabriel (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/jesse-gabriel-160858), an Encino Democrat, and Assembly Appropriations Vice Chair Josh Hoover (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/josh-hoover-165420), a Folsom Republican and the only GOP lawmaker to vote for the measure. Most Republican lawmakers opposed Prop. 2, stating that the state should use its excess revenue to give taxpayers refunds instead of saving it. They argue that state government already spends too much and that a bigger reserve would merely give state leaders more to spend. “When they say we’re here for fiscal responsibility, it’s like the devil offering a Bible study. Don’t buy it,” said (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/hearings/279785#t=685&f=074f023444d682ecc1d857e24642a263) Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/carl-demaio-161014), a San Diego Republican. How long have we had a rainy day fund? Before 2014, California leaders and voters established reserve funds several times (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5028) to weather financial storms, but ended up quickly withdrawing most of those funds, leaving the state with very little savings on hand, according to the legislative analyst. In 2004, following the dot-com bust, voters overwhelmingly supported Prop. 58, a bipartisan ballot measure (https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2004-feb-10-me-dems10-story.htm) that required the state to establish a budget stabilization account and make annual deposits into the fund. Sign up for free Δ But lawmakers swiftly depleted the fund during the early months of the Great Recession and were forced to make steep spending cuts, borrow money at expensive rates and use accounting gimmicks to weather the rest of the crisis. Under then-Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, a Republican, the state Legislature slashed health and welfare funding, scrapped tax credits, furloughed state employees (https://web.archive.org/web/20090809224605/http://www.dpa.ca.gov/news/news/2008/20081106-01.htm) and delayed payments (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2018/3910/recession-recovery-121318.pdf) to schools and local governments. In 2014, as the state’s economy rebounded, then-Gov. Jerry Brown, a Democrat, urged that the state save more. He and the Legislature championed Prop. 2, a bipartisan ballot measure that required the state to save more aggressively and limited when lawmakers could withdraw from the reserves. Nearly 70% of voters approved it. “When the pendulum swings again, we won’t be forced to raise taxes or make the kinds of harsh cuts that were all too common in recent years,” Brown said in a 2014 op-ed (https://www.sfgate.com/politics/article/Jerry-Brown-preaches-for-Prop-2-by-talking-up-5812922.php) stumping for the reform. The law requires the state to set aside 1.5% of its general fund revenue and any spikes in capital gains tax revenue each year, with half deposited into the reserves and the other half to pay down state debts. It also made it harder for the state to spend the reserves and carved out portions of the savings for schools. Under the law (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&division&title&part&chapter&article=XVI), state lawmakers can withdraw from the reserves only when the governor declares a budget emergency and decides that the state is not expected to collect enough revenue in the upcoming fiscal year to match the spending in the three previous budget years. A majority of state lawmakers must vote to ratify the budget emergency. If approved, they are allowed to withdraw up to half of the rainy day fund balance at once, unless they already withdrew half the balance in the previous budget year and still need to take out more. There are no limits on what lawmakers can use the funds for. Bigger reserve = more to spend? Prop. 2 would maintain those withdrawal rules, which critics say would give future governors broad authority to spend down the reserves instead of reining in spending. “The rainy day fund can be invaded even when it’s not raining, simply because spending isn’t as high as it was within the prior three years,” wrote David Crane (https://sfstandard.com/opinion/2026/09/14/newsom-rainy-day-fund-prop-2/), a former economic adviser to Schwarzenegger and founder of Govern for California, a nonprofit fundraising powerhouse (https://calmatters.org/politics/2022/08/california-campaign-finance-donor-network/) that aims to “counter special interest influence.” “Unless the withdrawal rules change, a larger reserve just lets governors bake in spending based on optimistic forecasts, knowing they can always dip into reserves if revenue falls short.” In an interview with CalMatters, Gabriel stressed that voters approved those rules in 2014 and emphasized that the measure has bipartisan support. He also dismissed the criticism that the state should just spend less during downturns, likening it to telling families to eat less or downsize instead of dipping into their savings when they fall on hard times. “I think (the concern) is very misplaced,” he said. “(Prop. 2) is recommended by the experts, because it matches the common-sense wisdom of California families.” READ NEXT What to know about California’s other tax-the-rich measure: Prop. 3 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-3-california/) October 21, 2026 This institute could get $4 billion from a ballot measure. The question Proposition 2 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-2-rainy-day-fund/) poses to California voters is simple: Should the state be able to save more money when its economy is booming? The ballot measure, dubbed the Save for California’s Future Act (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260aca20), seeks to shore up California’s rainy day fund by allowing state lawmakers to sock away up to 20% of the state’s general fund tax revenue — double the current ceiling of 10%. It would also require the state to save a bigger share of the gains when revenue is growing faster. Proponents, including Gov. Gavin Newsom and Democratic lawmakers, say the state needs a bigger savings account to weather its volatile economy. Because California’s tax revenue depends so much on wealthy residents’ stock earnings, the state budget is often caught in a boom-or-bust cycle (https://calmatters.org/explainers/california-budget-whiplash/) at the mercy of the market. In recent years, the state has seen robust tax revenue from an AI-fueled economy, which has helped state leaders avoid or delay painful cuts (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/05/gavin-newsom-final-budget-plan/) to social services even when they projected significant deficits. But economists have consistently warned the boom may not last, and the federal budget cuts to healthcare and welfare programs this year deepened that uncertainty. This voter guide has everything you need to know Supporters pitched Prop. 2 as a common sense solution, noting the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office, which advises state lawmakers, has long recommended the state set aside funding for downturns. The measure is endorsed by a bipartisan coalition of groups (https://www.yesonprop2.com/#endorsements), including labor unions, hospital associations and chambers of commerce. “It doubles the size of the state’s rainy day fund and requires California to save more during strong budget years, so we’re not caught flat-footed when the next downturn hits,” wrote (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/10/rainy-day-fund-california-proposition/) Assembly Budget Chair Jesse Gabriel (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/jesse-gabriel-160858), an Encino Democrat, and Assembly Appropriations Vice Chair Josh Hoover (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/josh-hoover-165420), a Folsom Republican and the only GOP lawmaker to vote for the measure. Most Republican lawmakers opposed Prop. 2, stating that the state should use its excess revenue to give taxpayers refunds instead of saving it. They argue that state government already spends too much and that a bigger reserve would merely give state leaders more to spend. “When they say we’re here for fiscal responsibility, it’s like the devil offering a Bible study. Don’t buy it,” said (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/hearings/279785#t=685&f=074f023444d682ecc1d857e24642a263) Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/carl-demaio-161014), a San Diego Republican. How long have we had a rainy day fund? Before 2014, California leaders and voters established reserve funds several times (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5028) to weather financial storms, but ended up quickly withdrawing most of those funds, leaving the state with very little savings on hand, according to the legislative analyst. In 2004, following the dot-com bust, voters overwhelmingly supported Prop. 58, a bipartisan ballot measure (https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2004-feb-10-me-dems10-story.htm) that required the state to establish a budget stabilization account and make annual deposits into the fund. Sign up for free Δ But lawmakers swiftly depleted the fund during the early months of the Great Recession and were forced to make steep spending cuts, borrow money at expensive rates and use accounting gimmicks to weather the rest of the crisis. Under then-Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, a Republican, the state Legislature slashed health and welfare funding, scrapped tax credits, furloughed state employees (https://web.archive.org/web/20090809224605/http://www.dpa.ca.gov/news/news/2008/20081106-01.htm) and delayed payments (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2018/3910/recession-recovery-121318.pdf) to schools and local governments. In 2014, as the state’s economy rebounded, then-Gov. Jerry Brown, a Democrat, urged that the state save more. He and the Legislature championed Prop. 2, a bipartisan ballot measure that required the state to save more aggressively and limited when lawmakers could withdraw from the reserves. Nearly 70% of voters approved it. “When the pendulum swings again, we won’t be forced to raise taxes or make the kinds of harsh cuts that were all too common in recent years,” Brown said in a 2014 op-ed (https://www.sfgate.com/politics/article/Jerry-Brown-preaches-for-Prop-2-by-talking-up-5812922.php) stumping for the reform. The law requires the state to set aside 1.5% of its general fund revenue and any spikes in capital gains tax revenue each year, with half deposited into the reserves and the other half to pay down state debts. It also made it harder for the state to spend the reserves and carved out portions of the savings for schools. Under the law (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&division&title&part&chapter&article=XVI), state lawmakers can withdraw from the reserves only when the governor declares a budget emergency and decides that the state is not expected to collect enough revenue in the upcoming fiscal year to match the spending in the three previous budget years. A majority of state lawmakers must vote to ratify the budget emergency. If approved, they are allowed to withdraw up to half of the rainy day fund balance at once, unless they already withdrew half the balance in the previous budget year and still need to take out more. There are no limits on what lawmakers can use the funds for. Bigger reserve = more to spend? Prop. 2 would maintain those withdrawal rules, which critics say would give future governors broad authority to spend down the reserves instead of reining in spending. “The rainy day fund can be invaded even when it’s not raining, simply because spending isn’t as high as it was within the prior three years,” wrote David Crane (https://sfstandard.com/opinion/2026/09/14/newsom-rainy-day-fund-prop-2/), a former economic adviser to Schwarzenegger and founder of Govern for California, a nonprofit fundraising powerhouse (https://calmatters.org/politics/2022/08/california-campaign-finance-donor-network/) that aims to “counter special interest influence.” “Unless the withdrawal rules change, a larger reserve just lets governors bake in spending based on optimistic forecasts, knowing they can always dip into reserves if revenue falls short.” In an interview with CalMatters, Gabriel stressed that voters approved those rules in 2014 and emphasized that the measure has bipartisan support. He also dismissed the criticism that the state should just spend less during downturns, likening it to telling families to eat less or downsize instead of dipping into their savings when they fall on hard times. “I think (the concern) is very misplaced,” he said. “(Prop. 2) is recommended by the experts, because it matches the common-sense wisdom of California families.” READ NEXT What to know about California’s other tax-the-rich measure: Prop. 3 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-3-california/) October 21, 2026 This institute could get $4 billion from a ballot measure. Proposition 2
Raise limit on rainy day fund deposits
This constitutional amendment would allow the state to deposit up to 20% of its general fund tax revenue in the state’s reserves, up from the current ceiling of 10%. The deposits would not count toward the voter-approved Gann Limit, which caps the amount state lawmakers can spend each year and requires excess funds to be returned to the people. It also authorizes spending some tax revenue to pay down California’s $20 billion federal unemployment insurance debt. The California Legislature placed this measure on the ballot.

Proposition 2
Raise limit on rainy day fund deposits
This constitutional amendment would allow the state to deposit up to 20% of its general fund tax revenue in the state’s reserves, up from the current ceiling of 10%. The deposits would not count toward the voter-approved Gann Limit, which caps the amount state lawmakers can spend each year and requires excess funds to be returned to the people. It also authorizes spending some tax revenue to pay down California’s $20 billion federal unemployment insurance debt. The California Legislature placed this measure on the ballot.

Guest Commentary written by Jesse Gabriel Jesse Gabriel, a Democrat from Encino, represents California’s 46th Assembly District and chairs the Assembly Budget Committee. Josh Hoover Josh Hoover, a Republican from Folsom, represents California’s 7th Assembly District and is vice chair of the Assembly Appropriations Committee. At a moment when Californians can’t agree on much, we’ve found common ground on something that matters: how the state saves for hard times. One of us is a Democrat. The other is a Republican. We are united about Proposition 2 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-2-rainy-day-fund/), because this measure isn’t about partisan politics. It’s about basic fiscal responsibility, and it was developed by the people who understand California’s budget best. California has one of the largest and most dynamic economies in the world. It’s also one of the most volatile (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/01/volatility-complicates-california-budget-deficits/). The state ranks fifth in the nation in revenue volatility (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5028) because of our tax structure, but only 29th in the size of its budget reserves. When the good times roll, state revenue pours in. When the economy faces challenges, the state is often forced into abrupt, painful cuts to programs Californians rely on: healthcare (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/08/the-cut-medi-cal-ripple-effects/), higher education, public safety and safety net services. Seniors, students and working families (https://calmatters.org/education/2026/08/head-start-california-2/) bear the brunt, often with little warning. Prop. 2 fixes that imbalance. It doubles the size of the state’s rainy day fund and requires California to save more during strong budget years, so we’re not caught flat-footed when the next downturn hits. This is a structural budget fix without raising taxes to save more. It’s the type of budgetary planning we need to protect our future. This isn’t a new or radical idea. It builds directly on a framework voters approved in 2014 (https://www.pew.org/-/media/assets/2014/06/californiarainydayfundanalysis.pdf). And it reflects more than a decade of experience with how that fund has actually worked. ELECTION 2026 (https://calmatters.org/tag/election-2026) 2026 Voter Guide (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/) Get ready for California’s midterm election. This voter guide has everything you need to know Prop. 2 didn’t start with politicians. It was born from budget experts, not special interests. The Legislative Analyst’s Office, California’s nonpartisan fiscal watchdog, recommended its reforms, which developed during legislative hearings with input from the Department of Finance, independent fiscal experts and business leaders. But its earliest supporters were firefighters, small business advocates, healthcare providers and education leaders — people who see firsthand what happens when reserves run dry and cuts land on hospitals, schools (https://calmatters.org/education/k-12-education/2026/06/school-libraries-california/) and emergency response. That list has since grown because state leaders and fiscal experts from across the political spectrum have lived through what happens when California doesn’t save enough. A stronger rainy day fund would make California more fiscally credible to taxpayers. States that save responsibly don’t just weather downturns better; they also borrow more cheaply and give families and businesses more confidence that the state can keep its commitments, even when the economy turns. That’s the real case for Prop 2. California is safer, steadier and more trustworthy when it saves like it means it. Saving responsibly is not a partisan value. It’s common sense. California’s budget shouldn’t lurch from boom to bust. Prop. 2 gives us a better way forward. One area Democrats, GOP agree: California needs a larger rainy day fund

By Jesse Gabriel and Josh Hoover, Special for CalMatters

This commentary was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

Guest Commentary written by

At a moment when Californians can't agree on much, we've found common ground on something that matters: how the state saves for hard times.

One of us is a Democrat. The other is a Republican. We are united about Proposition 2, because this measure isn't about partisan politics. It's about basic fiscal responsibility, and it was developed by the people who understand California's budget best.

California has one of the largest and most dynamic economies in the world. It's also one of the most volatile. The state ranks fifth in the nation in revenue volatility because of our tax structure, but only 29th in the size of its budget reserves.

When the good times roll, state revenue pours in. When the economy faces challenges, the state is often forced into abrupt, painful cuts to programs Californians rely on: healthcare, higher education, public safety and safety net services.

Seniors, students and working families bear the brunt, often with little warning.

Prop. 2 fixes that imbalance. It doubles the size of the state's rainy day fund and requires California to save more during strong budget years, so we're not caught flat-footed when the next downturn hits.

This is a structural budget fix without raising taxes to save more. It’s the type of budgetary planning we need to protect our future.

This isn't a new or radical idea. It builds directly on a framework voters approved in 2014. And it reflects more than a decade of experience with how that fund has actually worked.

Prop. 2 didn’t start with politicians. It was born from budget experts, not special interests. 

The Legislative Analyst's Office, California's nonpartisan fiscal watchdog, recommended its reforms, which developed during legislative hearings with input from the Department of Finance, independent fiscal experts and business leaders.

But its earliest supporters were firefighters, small business advocates, healthcare providers and education leaders — people who see firsthand what happens when reserves run dry and cuts land on hospitals, schools and emergency response. 

That list has since grown because state leaders and fiscal experts from across the political spectrum have lived through what happens when California doesn't save enough.

A stronger rainy day fund would make California more fiscally credible to taxpayers. States that save responsibly don't just weather downturns better; they also borrow more cheaply and give families and businesses more confidence that the state can keep its commitments, even when the economy turns. 

That's the real case for Prop 2. California is safer, steadier and more trustworthy when it saves like it means it.

Saving responsibly is not a partisan value. It's common sense. California's budget shouldn't lurch from boom to bust. Prop. 2 gives us a better way forward.

PROPOSITION 2
This amendment proposed by Assembly Constitutional
Amendment 20 of the 2025–2026 Regular Session
(Resolution Chapter 130, Statutes of 2026) expressly
amends the California Constitution by amending
sections thereof; therefore, existing provisions
proposed to be deleted are printed in strikeout type
and new provisions proposed to be added are printed in
italic type to indicate that they are new.
2
PROPOSED AMENDMENTS TO ARTICLE XVI
First—(a) This measure shall be known, and may be
cited, as the Save for California’s Future Act.
(b) The Legislature finds and declares all of the
following:
(1) California families understand that responsible
financial planning requires setting aside savings during
good times to prepare for unexpected challenges and
economic downturns. The State of California should
follow the same commonsense principle.
(2) Californians expect their government to manage
public finances responsibly, prudently, and with an eye
toward future generations. Maintaining adequate
reserves helps ensure that essential public services
remain available when they are needed most.
(3) California’s economy is among the largest and
most dynamic in the world, but it is also subject to
economic cycles, fluctuations in revenue, natural
disasters, public health emergencies, and other
unforeseen events that can place significant strain on
the state budget.
(4) When state revenues decline during economic
downturns, insufficient reserves can force difficult
choices that disrupt essential programs and services
relied upon by California families, students, seniors,
veterans, workers, and businesses.
(5) Building and maintaining strong budget reserves
during periods of economic growth helps protect
Californians from sudden reductions in essential
services and reduces the need for drastic corrective
actions during periods of fiscal stress.
(6) Sound financial planning requires looking beyond
the next fiscal year and preparing for future challenges
before they arise. Just like families save for
emergencies and unexpected expenses, California
should save during good years to protect schools,
public safety, and essential services during tough
times.
(7) Strong reserve policies promote fiscal stability,
improve public confidence in state government,
support long-term economic growth, and help preserve
California’s ability to respond effectively to
emergencies and economic downturns.
(8) Proposition 98 was enacted by the voters in 1988
to provide a minimum funding level for schools. Nothing
in this act is intended to change the calculation or
106 | Text of Proposed Laws
funding of the minimum guarantee under Section 8 of
Article XVI.
(c) It is therefore the intent of the Legislature to
strengthen the state’s commitment to responsible
budgeting, long-term financial planning, and prudent
savings by enhancing California’s budget reserves and
ensuring that the state is better prepared for future
economic challenges. Strengthening reserves is an
investment in California’s future and in future
generations.
Second—That Section 20 of Article XVI thereof is
amended to read:
SEC. 20. (a) (1) (A) The Budget Stabilization
Account is hereby created in the General Fund.
(B) Balances deposited in the Budget Stabilization
Account pursuant to paragraph (2) of this subdivision
(a) and subdivisions (c) and (d) prior to the effective
date of the measure adding this subparagraph shall
remain in the account and shall be transferred,
withdrawn, or adjusted thereafter pursuant to the
provisions of this Constitution as amended by the
measure adding this subparagraph.
(2) For the 2015–16 2027–28 fiscal year and each
fiscal year thereafter, based on the Budget Act for the
fiscal year, the Controller shall transfer from the
General Fund to the Budget Stabilization Account, no
later than October 1, a sum equal to 1.5 percent of the
estimated amount of General Fund revenues for that
fiscal year.
(b) (1) For the 2015–16 2027–28 fiscal year and
each fiscal year thereafter, based on the Budget Act for
the fiscal year, the Department of Finance shall provide
to the Legislature all of the following information:
(A) An estimate of the amount of General Fund
proceeds of taxes that may be appropriated pursuant
to Article XIII B for that fiscal year.
(B) (i) An estimate of that portion of the General Fund
proceeds of taxes identified in subparagraph (A) that is
derived from personal income taxes paid on net capital
gains.
(ii) The sum of the following:
(ii) (I) The portion of the estimate in clause (i) that
exceeds 8 percent of is in excess of 8 percent, but not
in excess of 10 percent, of the estimate made under
subparagraph (A).
(II) One hundred fifty percent of the portion of the
estimate in clause (i) in excess of 10 percent of the
estimate made under subparagraph (A).
(C) That portion of the state’s funding obligation under
Section 8 that results from including the amount
calculated under clause (ii) of subparagraph (B), if any,
as General Fund proceeds of taxes.
(D) The amount of any appropriations described in
clause (ii) of subparagraph (B) of paragraph (1) of, or
subparagraph (C) of paragraph (2) of, subdivision (c),
that are made from the revenues described in clause
(ii) of subparagraph (B) of this paragraph.

(E) The amount resulting from subtracting the
combined values calculated under subparagraphs (C)
and (D) from the value calculated under clause (ii) of
subparagraph (B). If less than zero, the amount shall be
considered zero for this purpose.
(F) The lesser of the amount calculated under
subparagraph (E) or the amount of transfer resulting in
the balance in the Budget Stabilization Account
reaching the limit specified in subdivision (e).
(2) In the 2016–17 2027–28 fiscal year, with respect
to the 2015–16 2026–27 fiscal year only, and in the
2017–18 2028–29 fiscal year and each fiscal year
thereafter, separately with respect to each of the two
next preceding fiscal years, the Department of Finance
shall calculate all of the following, using the same
methodology used for the relevant fiscal year, and
provide those calculations to the Legislature:
(A) An updated estimate of the amount of General
Fund proceeds of taxes that may be appropriated
pursuant to Article XIII B.
(B) (i) An updated estimate of that portion of the
General Fund proceeds of taxes identified in
subparagraph (A) that is derived from personal income
taxes paid on net capital gains.
(ii) The sum of the following:
(ii) (I) That portion of the updated estimate in clause

but not in excess of 10 percent, of the updated estimate
made under subparagraph (A).
(II) One hundred fifty percent of the portion of the
estimate in clause (i) in excess of 10 percent of the
estimate made under subparagraph (A).
(C) The updated calculation of that portion of the
state’s funding obligation under Section 8 that results

proceeds of taxes.
(D) The amount of any appropriations described in
clause (ii) of subparagraph (B) of paragraph (1) of, or
subparagraph (C) of paragraph (2) of, subdivision (c),
that are made from the revenues described in clause
(ii) of subparagraph (B) of paragraph (1).
(E) The amount resulting from subtracting the
combined values calculated under subparagraphs (C)
and (D) from the value calculated under clause (ii) of
subparagraph (B). If less than zero, the amount shall be
considered zero for this purpose.
(F) The amount previously transferred for the fiscal
year by the Controller from the General Fund to the
Budget Stabilization Account pursuant to subdivisions
(c) and (d).
(G) The lesser of (i) the amount, not less than zero,
resulting from subtracting, from the amount calculated
under subparagraph (E), the value of any suspension or
reduction of transfer pursuant to paragraph (1) of
subdivision (a) of Section 22 previously approved by
the Legislature for the relevant fiscal year, and the
amount previously transferred for that fiscal year by the
Controller as described in subparagraph (F), or (ii) the
amount of transfer resulting in the balance in the
Budget Stabilization Account reaching the limit as
specified in subdivision (e).
(c) (1) (A) By October 1 of the 2015–16 2027–28
fiscal year and each fiscal year thereafter to the 2029–
30 2039–40 fiscal year, inclusive, based on the
estimates set forth in the annual Budget Act pursuant
to paragraphs (2) and (3) of subdivision (h), and the
sum identified in paragraph (2) of subdivision (a), the
Controller shall transfer amounts from the General
Fund and the Budget Stabilization Account, pursuant
to a schedule provided by the Director of Finance, as
provided in subparagraph (B).
(B) Notwithstanding any other provision of this section,
in the fiscal year to which the Budget Act identified in
subparagraph (A) applies:
(i) Fifty percent of both the amount identified in
paragraph (2) of subdivision (a), and the amount
resulting from subtracting the value calculated under
subparagraph (C) of paragraph (1) of subdivision (b)
from the value calculated under clause (ii) of
subparagraph (B) of paragraph (1) of subdivision (b),
shall be transferred from the General Fund to the
Budget Stabilization Account.
(ii) The remaining 50 percent shall be appropriated by
the Legislature for one or more of the following
obligations and purposes:
(I) Unfunded prior fiscal year General Fund obligations
pursuant to Section 8 that existed on July 1, 2014. 8.
(II) Budgetary loans to the General Fund, from funds
outside the General Fund, that had outstanding
balances on January 1, 2014. as well as earlier than
scheduled recognition of the costs of loans made to the
Medical Providers Interim Payment Fund and earlier
than scheduled recognition of costs described in
paragraph (1) of subdivision (c) of Section 41206.04 of
the Education Code.
(III) Payable claims for mandated costs incurred prior
to the 2004–05 fiscal year that have not yet been paid,
and that pursuant to paragraph (2) of subdivision (b) of
Section 6 of Article XIII B are permitted to be paid over
a term of years, as prescribed by law.
(IV) Unfunded liabilities for state-level pension plans
and prefunding other postemployment benefits, in
excess of current base amounts as established for the
fiscal year in which the funds would otherwise be
transferred to the Budget Stabilization Account. For the
purpose of this subclause, current base amounts are
those required to be paid pursuant to law, an approved
memorandum of understanding, benefit schedules
established by the employer or entity authorized to
establish those contributions for employees excluded
or exempted from collective bargaining, or any
combination of these. To qualify under this subclause,
the appropriation shall supplement and not supplant
funding that would otherwise be made available to pay
for the obligations described in this subclause for the
fiscal year or the subsequent fiscal year.

Proposition 2
Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
Analysis of Measure
Background
The State Budget
How Does the State Spend Its Money? This year, the state plans to spend about $250 billion from the General Fund to pay for services to the public. The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services. About half of this spending is for schools, community colleges, and the state's public universities. (The State Constitution sets a minimum spending level for schools and community colleges.) About another one-third of state spending is for health and human services programs, mainly for the state's low-income health insurance program, Medi-Cal. The rest goes mostly to prisons, courts, and other state services.
How Does the State Raise Revenue? The income tax is the state's largest tax. It pays for most spending from the General Fund. Other major taxes include the corporation tax and the sales tax. Much of the income tax is paid by high-income taxpayers, whose incomes often include gains from stocks and other investments.
State Revenues Are Unpredictable. State revenues go up and down a lot from year to year. This is because revenues depend on how the economy and stock market are doing. When things are going well, revenues can grow quickly. When things are going badly, like during a recession or a stock market crash, revenues can decline by tens of billions of dollars. During a bad recession or market crash, total revenue declines over a few years can equal 50 percent or more of annual General Fund revenues.
The State Must Meet Certain Budgeting Requirements Each Year. The State Constitution requires the Legislature to pass a balanced budget each year. This means the state cannot adopt a budget that spends more money than is available. In addition, the State Constitution limits how much tax revenue the state can spend. This limit is called the "state appropriations limit." Certain kinds of spending-like infrastructure-do not count toward the limit. All other spending, including money put into reserves, does count toward the limit.
Reserves
Reserves Allow the State to Maintain Spending When Revenues Decline. The state puts money into reserves when the economy is doing well. This means that money is saved instead of being spent on public programs during these periods of time. When the economy gets worse and revenues decline, the state uses reserves to help maintain spending on public programs. Reserves help the state avoid some spending cuts, tax increases, and borrowing to balance the budget. Currently, the state has about $20 billion in reserves that can be used for any public program.
State Constitution Requires the State to Save Money in the "Rainy Day Fund." The State Constitution requires the state to deposit 0.75 percent of General Fund tax revenues in the state's main rainy day fund, which is called the Budget Stabilization Account, each year. Money in the rainy day fund can be used for any state program. In addition, the state must put more money into the rainy day fund in years when revenue from taxes on investment gains is higher than normal. During a budget emergency, the state can stop making deposits and/or take money out of the rainy day fund.
Savings Are No Longer Required Once the Rainy Day Fund Reaches a Certain Level. Once money in the rainy day fund reaches 10 percent of General Fund taxes, the state is no longer required to make additional deposits. The money that would have gone into the rainy day fund instead must be spent on infrastructure (like highways and housing).
Debt
The State Has Different Kinds of Debts. The state has more than $250 billion in debts. These include debt for infrastructure and pension and retiree health benefits earned by state employees. The state also sometimes borrows money from other state funds to help pay General Fund costs. State debts are repaid over time, usually according to a schedule or plan. Each year, the state makes payments toward its debts.
State Constitution Requires the State to Make Extra Debt Payments Toward Pension and Health Benefits. The State Constitution requires the state to make extra debt payments above those normally made each year. The amount of these extra debt payments is the same as the amount initially deposited into the rainy day fund each year. The state may only use these extra debt payments to pay down long-term pension and retiree health care debts. Making extra payments toward these debts saves the state money in the long run.
Extra Debt Payments Optional After 2030. The requirement for extra debt payments ends in 2030. After that, the Legislature and the Governor could decide to deposit the money for extra debt payments into the rainy day fund instead. Or, the Legislature and the Governor could make smaller extra debt payments and put the rest of the money into the rainy day fund.
Proposal
Save More in the Rainy Day Fund. Proposition 2 requires the state to make deposits into the rainy day fund until it reaches 20 percent of General Fund taxes (instead of 10 percent of General Fund taxes). In addition, the state would make even larger deposits in years when revenues from taxes on investment gains are very high, like when the stock market is booming.
Extend and Expand Extra Debt Payments. Proposition 2 also requires the state to make extra debt payments through 2040 (instead of through 2030). These debt payments would be the same as the amount initially deposited into the rainy day fund each year. In addition, the amount set aside for extra debt payments could be used for an expanded set of purposes. Specifically, these payments could be used to make required payments to schools and community colleges, repay borrowing from other state funds, and repay certain loans from the federal government.
Change How Rainy Day Fund Deposits Count Toward the State Appropriations Limit. Deposits into the rainy day fund would not count toward the state appropriations limit. Instead, the money would count toward the limit when it is taken out.
Change How Other Deposits Count Toward the State Appropriations Limit. The state has an account to set aside funds when revenues are surging. By setting these funds aside, the state can avoid overspending when revenue estimates are particularly uncertain. Under Proposition 2, deposits into this account also would not count toward the state appropriations limit. Instead, the money would count toward the limit when it is taken out. This exclusion could not be larger than 10 percent of General Fund taxes in each year.
Fiscal Effects
Budget Reserves Would Be Higher. By continuing to require deposits into the rainy day fund until the balance reaches 20 percent of General Fund taxes, the state would save more over time. In addition, by depositing more money when revenues are surging, the state likely would save more in the rainy day fund in certain years. More reserves would make balancing the budget somewhat easier when revenues decline.
Possibly More Debt Payments. By requiring the state to make extra debt payments through 2040, the state might make more debt payments than it would without Proposition 2.
Yes/No Statement
A YES vote on this measure means: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would change. As a result, state budget reserves would be higher. The state also would be required to make extra debt payments for longer.
A NO vote on this measure means: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would not change.
Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact
State budget reserves would be higher.

Proposition 2: Rainy Day Fund
Proposition 2: Rainy Day Fund
Proposition 2: Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund. Legislative Constitutional Amendment
Additional Titles
Budget Stabilization Account Cap Increase and Gann Limit Changes Amendment
Rainy day Fund
Raise limit on rainy day fund deposits
Summary
Proposition 2 was placed on the ballot by the California Legislature as Assembly Constitutional Amendment 20 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA20&utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email) The amendment was introduced on June 25, 2026 and it passed the state Assembly by a vote of 59-8, with 12 not voting. It passed the state Senate by a vote of 29-2, with nine not voting.
Proposition 2 on the November 2026 ballot would amend the State Constitution (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codesTOCSelected.xhtml?tocCode=CONS&tocTitle=+California+Constitution+-+CONS) by changing California’s rainy day fund rules to build larger reserves and better protect public services during economic downturns and other budget emergencies. Specifically, it would require the state to make deposits into the fund until it reaches 20 percent of General Fund taxes (instead of the current 10 percent of General Fund taxes).
It would also expand the types of state debt that can be repaid with General Fund money set aside each year and require the extra debt payments through 2040 (instead of the current date of 2030). In addition, Prop. 2 would change how certain reserves are treated under the state spending cap, or “Gann Limit (https://www.cde.ca.gov/fg/ac/gl/),” making it easier to save more money when revenues are strong. The Legislature placed the constitutional amendment on the ballot through Assembly Constitutional Amendment 20 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA20).
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 2 would allow California to build a larger financial cushion by raising the maximum size of the state’s rainy day fund. It would also direct a greater share of unusually strong revenues into savings during high-revenue years. Having more money set aside could give the state greater flexibility during economic downturns or other periods when tax collections fall short of expectations.
Proposition 2 would extend requirements for additional state debt payments through 2040. As a result, California could pay down more of its outstanding debts and long-term financial obligations than it otherwise would under current rules.
What your vote means
YES: A “yes” vote supports changing California’s rainy day fund rules to allow larger reserves, increase deposits when revenues are strong, extend required debt payments through 2040, and change how certain reserves are treated under the state spending limit. It would also allow the governor’s May budget revision to serve as a declaration of a budget emergency when certain conditions are met.
NO: A “no” vote opposes these changes and would keep the current rules for the state’s rainy day fund, extra debt payments, spending limit, and declarations of budget emergencies.

Critics say it would only allow state leaders to spend more in the future. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. The question Proposition 2 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-2-rainy-day-fund/) poses to California voters is simple: Should the state be able to save more money when its economy is booming? The ballot measure, dubbed the Save for California’s Future Act (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260aca20), seeks to shore up California’s rainy day fund by allowing state lawmakers to sock away up to 20% of the state’s general fund tax revenue — double the current ceiling of 10%. It would also require the state to save a bigger share of the gains when revenue is growing faster. Proponents, including Gov. Gavin Newsom and Democratic lawmakers, say the state needs a bigger savings account to weather its volatile economy. Because California’s tax revenue depends so much on wealthy residents’ stock earnings, the state budget is often caught in a boom-or-bust cycle (https://calmatters.org/explainers/california-budget-whiplash/) at the mercy of the market. In recent years, the state has seen robust tax revenue from an AI-fueled economy, which has helped state leaders avoid or delay painful cuts (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/05/gavin-newsom-final-budget-plan/) to social services even when they projected significant deficits. But economists have consistently warned the boom may not last, and the federal budget cuts to healthcare and welfare programs this year deepened that uncertainty. This voter guide has everything you need to know Supporters pitched Prop. 2 as a common sense solution, noting the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office, which advises state lawmakers, has long recommended the state set aside funding for downturns. The measure is endorsed by a bipartisan coalition of groups (https://www.yesonprop2.com/#endorsements), including labor unions, hospital associations and chambers of commerce. “It doubles the size of the state’s rainy day fund and requires California to save more during strong budget years, so we’re not caught flat-footed when the next downturn hits,” wrote (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/10/rainy-day-fund-california-proposition/) Assembly Budget Chair Jesse Gabriel (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/jesse-gabriel-160858), an Encino Democrat, and Assembly Appropriations Vice Chair Josh Hoover (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/josh-hoover-165420), a Folsom Republican and the only GOP lawmaker to vote for the measure. Most Republican lawmakers opposed Prop. 2, stating that the state should use its excess revenue to give taxpayers refunds instead of saving it. They argue that state government already spends too much and that a bigger reserve would merely give state leaders more to spend. “When they say we’re here for fiscal responsibility, it’s like the devil offering a Bible study. Don’t buy it,” said (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/hearings/279785#t=685&f=074f023444d682ecc1d857e24642a263) Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/carl-demaio-161014), a San Diego Republican. How long have we had a rainy day fund? Before 2014, California leaders and voters established reserve funds several times (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5028) to weather financial storms, but ended up quickly withdrawing most of those funds, leaving the state with very little savings on hand, according to the legislative analyst. In 2004, following the dot-com bust, voters overwhelmingly supported Prop. 58, a bipartisan ballot measure (https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2004-feb-10-me-dems10-story.htm) that required the state to establish a budget stabilization account and make annual deposits into the fund. Sign up for free Δ But lawmakers swiftly depleted the fund during the early months of the Great Recession and were forced to make steep spending cuts, borrow money at expensive rates and use accounting gimmicks to weather the rest of the crisis. Under then-Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, a Republican, the state Legislature slashed health and welfare funding, scrapped tax credits, furloughed state employees (https://web.archive.org/web/20090809224605/http://www.dpa.ca.gov/news/news/2008/20081106-01.htm) and delayed payments (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2018/3910/recession-recovery-121318.pdf) to schools and local governments. In 2014, as the state’s economy rebounded, then-Gov. Jerry Brown, a Democrat, urged that the state save more. He and the Legislature championed Prop. 2, a bipartisan ballot measure that required the state to save more aggressively and limited when lawmakers could withdraw from the reserves. Nearly 70% of voters approved it. “When the pendulum swings again, we won’t be forced to raise taxes or make the kinds of harsh cuts that were all too common in recent years,” Brown said in a 2014 op-ed (https://www.sfgate.com/politics/article/Jerry-Brown-preaches-for-Prop-2-by-talking-up-5812922.php) stumping for the reform. The law requires the state to set aside 1.5% of its general fund revenue and any spikes in capital gains tax revenue each year, with half deposited into the reserves and the other half to pay down state debts. It also made it harder for the state to spend the reserves and carved out portions of the savings for schools. Under the law (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&division&title&part&chapter&article=XVI), state lawmakers can withdraw from the reserves only when the governor declares a budget emergency and decides that the state is not expected to collect enough revenue in the upcoming fiscal year to match the spending in the three previous budget years. A majority of state lawmakers must vote to ratify the budget emergency. If approved, they are allowed to withdraw up to half of the rainy day fund balance at once, unless they already withdrew half the balance in the previous budget year and still need to take out more. There are no limits on what lawmakers can use the funds for. Bigger reserve = more to spend? Prop. 2 would maintain those withdrawal rules, which critics say would give future governors broad authority to spend down the reserves instead of reining in spending. “The rainy day fund can be invaded even when it’s not raining, simply because spending isn’t as high as it was within the prior three years,” wrote David Crane (https://sfstandard.com/opinion/2026/09/14/newsom-rainy-day-fund-prop-2/), a former economic adviser to Schwarzenegger and founder of Govern for California, a nonprofit fundraising powerhouse (https://calmatters.org/politics/2022/08/california-campaign-finance-donor-network/) that aims to “counter special interest influence.” “Unless the withdrawal rules change, a larger reserve just lets governors bake in spending based on optimistic forecasts, knowing they can always dip into reserves if revenue falls short.” In an interview with CalMatters, Gabriel stressed that voters approved those rules in 2014 and emphasized that the measure has bipartisan support. He also dismissed the criticism that the state should just spend less during downturns, likening it to telling families to eat less or downsize instead of dipping into their savings when they fall on hard times. “I think (the concern) is very misplaced,” he said. “(Prop. 2) is recommended by the experts, because it matches the common-sense wisdom of California families.” READ NEXT What to know about California’s other tax-the-rich measure: Prop. 3 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-3-california/) October 21, 2026 This institute could get $4 billion from a ballot measure. Proposition 2
Raise limit on rainy day fund deposits
This constitutional amendment would allow the state to deposit up to 20% of its general fund tax revenue in the state’s reserves, up from the current ceiling of 10%. The deposits would not count toward the voter-approved Gann Limit, which caps the amount state lawmakers can spend each year and requires excess funds to be returned to the people. It also authorizes spending some tax revenue to pay down California’s $20 billion federal unemployment insurance debt. The California Legislature placed this measure on the ballot.

One area Democrats, GOP agree: California needs a larger rainy day fund

By Jesse Gabriel and Josh Hoover, Special for CalMatters

This commentary was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

Guest Commentary written by

At a moment when Californians can't agree on much, we've found common ground on something that matters: how the state saves for hard times.

One of us is a Democrat. The other is a Republican. We are united about Proposition 2, because this measure isn't about partisan politics. It's about basic fiscal responsibility, and it was developed by the people who understand California's budget best.

California has one of the largest and most dynamic economies in the world. It's also one of the most volatile. The state ranks fifth in the nation in revenue volatility because of our tax structure, but only 29th in the size of its budget reserves.

When the good times roll, state revenue pours in. When the economy faces challenges, the state is often forced into abrupt, painful cuts to programs Californians rely on: healthcare, higher education, public safety and safety net services.

Seniors, students and working families bear the brunt, often with little warning.

Prop. 2 fixes that imbalance. It doubles the size of the state's rainy day fund and requires California to save more during strong budget years, so we're not caught flat-footed when the next downturn hits.

This is a structural budget fix without raising taxes to save more. It’s the type of budgetary planning we need to protect our future.

This isn't a new or radical idea. It builds directly on a framework voters approved in 2014. And it reflects more than a decade of experience with how that fund has actually worked.

Prop. 2 didn’t start with politicians. It was born from budget experts, not special interests. 

The Legislative Analyst's Office, California's nonpartisan fiscal watchdog, recommended its reforms, which developed during legislative hearings with input from the Department of Finance, independent fiscal experts and business leaders.

But its earliest supporters were firefighters, small business advocates, healthcare providers and education leaders — people who see firsthand what happens when reserves run dry and cuts land on hospitals, schools and emergency response. 

That list has since grown because state leaders and fiscal experts from across the political spectrum have lived through what happens when California doesn't save enough.

A stronger rainy day fund would make California more fiscally credible to taxpayers. States that save responsibly don't just weather downturns better; they also borrow more cheaply and give families and businesses more confidence that the state can keep its commitments, even when the economy turns. 

That's the real case for Prop 2. California is safer, steadier and more trustworthy when it saves like it means it.

Saving responsibly is not a partisan value. It's common sense. California's budget shouldn't lurch from boom to bust. Prop. 2 gives us a better way forward.

***Proposition*** ***2 Contains Annual Debt Payment Requirement.*** Proposition 2 created new rules regarding: (1) deposits into the state’s rainy‑day fund and (2) accelerating payments toward certain eligible debts.
A formula dictates these requirements on an annual basis.
In general, the requirements tend to increase when revenues are growing more quickly and decline when revenue growth is lower.

## Proposition 2: Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund. Legislative Constitutional Amendment
### Summary
Proposition 2 was placed on the ballot by the California Legislature as Assembly Constitutional Amendment 20 The amendment was introduced on June 25, 2026 and it passed the state Assembly by a vote of 59-8, with 12 not voting.
It passed the state Senate by a vote of 29-2, with nine not voting.
Proposition 2 on the November 2026 ballot would amend the State Constitution by changing California’s rainy day fund rules to build larger reserves and better protect public services during economic downturns and other budget emergencies.
Specifically, it would require the state to make deposits into the fund until it reaches 20 percent of General Fund taxes (instead of the current 10 percent of General Fund taxes).
It would also expand the types of state debt that can be repaid with General Fund money set aside each year and require the extra debt payments through 2040 (instead of the current date of 2030).
In addition, Prop.
2 would change how certain reserves are treated under the state spending cap, or “Gann Limit,” making it easier to save more money when revenues are strong.
...

It would also direct a greater share of unusually strong revenues into savings during high-revenue years.

There is no one-size-fits-all rule on when, how, and how much to save.
